results.title: What is a neocloud, and how does it price GPUs?
results.author: The Hardware Desk
highlights:
A neocloud is a cloud provider, such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius or Crusoe, built entirely around renting Nvidia GPUs rather than general-purpose compute; it prices capacity on two tiers, a high hourly on-demand rate for flexibility and a discounted multi-year committed rate, with the gap (CoreWeave's HGX H100 runs $6.16 per GPU-hour on-demand versus up to 60% less reserved) funding the debt used to buy the GPUs in the first place.

...

A neocloud is a specialist cloud provider, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius and Crusoe are the four SemiAnalysis classified as “neocloud giants” in its October 2024 taxonomy, that sells GPU rental almost exclusively instead of the broad service catalog a hyperscaler like AWS or Azure bundles. Pricing runs on two tracks: an on-demand hourly rate priced for flexibility and idle-capacity risk, and a reserved or committed rate discounted against multi-year contracts, up to 60% off on CoreWeave’s own pricing page. A blended market rate sits below either extreme: Ornn Data’s H100 SXM index settled at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, versus CoreWeave’s $6.16 on-demand sticker for the same chip. The reserved discount exists because a signed, multi-year contract is exactly what lets a neocloud borrow money to buy the GPUs in the first place, so the price you’re quoted is really a reflection of how much certainty you’re giving the provider.

...

That single fact, an idle GPU costs money and an idle GPU earns nothing, explains the whole pricing structure. On-demand rates are set high because that customer is asking for maximum flexibility with zero commitment, so the provider prices in both the option value it’s giving up and the risk that the same hour goes unsold to someone else. Reserved or committed rates are set low because that customer is providing exactly what a lender wants to see: predictable, contracted cash flow over a multi-year term, the kind of backlog that let CoreWeave carry $99.4 billion in signed but not-yet-delivered revenue as of 2026-03-31. Spot pricing sits at the opposite extreme from on-demand: CoreWeave lists spot HGX H100 capacity at $19.71 an hour, 60% below its on-demand rate, because spot is explicitly the leftover capacity a provider would rather sell cheap than leave idle. The underlying Nvidia H100 silicon (What is a GPU?) doesn’t change between these tiers; only the certainty attached to the rental does.

...

The gap between on-demand and reserved pricing, and between one neocloud’s sticker price and the broader market, is the whole story. CoreWeave’s own pricing page lists three current Nvidia generations, each as an eight-GPU HGX node:

| GPU (8x HGX node) | On-demand, per node | On-demand, per GPU-hour | Spot, per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | $49.24/hr | $6.16 | $2.46 |
| H200 | $50.44/hr | $6.31 | $2.62 |
| B200 | $68.80/hr | $8.60 | $4.26 |

Lambda prices per GPU rather than per node: its H100 SXM runs $3.99 to $4.29 per GPU-hour on-demand and its B200 SXM6 runs $6.69 to $6.99, both lower than CoreWeave’s equivalent on-demand figures, which is consistent with Lambda competing on price within the same neocloud-giant tier. Against both of those sits Ornn Data’s blended H100 index, the same number that answers how much does it cost to rent an H100 per hour?, which settled at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, below every on-demand figure above because the index averages across many providers and contract structures, including the deep reserved discounts that never show up on a public on-demand rate card. CoreWeave doesn’t publish what those reserved rates actually are by term length or volume, only that committed usage saves “up to 60% over on-demand prices,” so the number a given customer pays sits somewhere between that index average and the on-demand ceiling depending entirely on what they’re willing to sign. Underneath all of this, CoreWeave reported $2.078 billion in Q1 2026 revenue and a 56% adjusted EBITDA margin against that $99.4 billion backlog, evidence that the reserved side of the business, not the on-demand sticker, is what actually funds the buildout.

...

The decision a buyer is actually making is how much certainty to trade for price, and the numbers above make that trade explicit rather than a vibe. A short training run, a burst inference workload, or a proof of concept has no business paying reserved rates, since it can’t offer the multi-year commitment that earns the discount, and it should expect to pay close to CoreWeave’s $6.16 on-demand H100 figure or shop Lambda’s lower on-demand rate instead. A sustained production workload, the kind running 24/7 for a year or more, is the workload the reserved discount was built for, and locking in a multi-year term against a specific GPU generation can plausibly get within range of Ornn Data’s $2.68 blended index rate, sometimes lower, depending on volume. Spot capacity is the third lever, and it’s the right call for anything genuinely interruptible: batch inference, checkpointed training, anything that can tolerate a GPU getting reclaimed mid-job in exchange for CoreWeave’s 60%-off spot rate. What a buyer should not do is compare a hyperscaler’s published on-demand price directly to a neocloud’s on-demand price and call it done, because the real comparison a large buyer makes is neocloud reserved pricing against hyperscaler committed-use discounts, and neither side publishes that number without a sales call.

results.title: Lambda Review, Pricing & Alternatives | Saaskly
highlights:
## What it costs

 Prices are in US dollars, VAT not stated, read 22 September 2026. Lambda charges per GPU per hour, and the rate goes up as you take fewer GPUs, which is the opposite of what most buyers expect. One H100 SXM 80 GB costs $4.29 an hour, or $3,132 a month at 730 hours. Take the whole eight-GPU node and the same GPU costs $3.99 an hour, so the node is $31.92 an hour and each GPU works out at $2,913 a month. Two and four GPU configurations sit in between at $4.19 and $4.09. An H100 PCIe is $3.29 an hour. The cheapest GPU on the list is a Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB at $0.69 an hour, about $504 a month, and a GH200 is $2.29. No H200 appears on the public price list at all, despite the pricing page's own marketing copy mentioning it. There is no spot, preemptible or interruptible tier, so there is no cheap way to buy compute you are willing to lose. Reserved pricing for a single on-demand instance is sales only: no rate, no term and no discount figure is published.

 The one published committed option is a 1-Click Cluster, and the arithmetic is counterintuitive. Sixteen H100s cost $6.16 per GPU-hour on a term of two weeks to a year, falling to $5.85 at 64 GPUs and $5.54 at 256. All three are higher than the $3.99 on-demand rate for an eight-GPU node, so a cluster buys InfiniBand and guaranteed capacity rather than a discount. The smallest cluster you can book is 16 GPUs for two weeks, roughly $33,100 paid up front, which puts it out of reach for most small teams. Storage is billed separately and keeps running after the instance has gone: the documentation gives $0.20 per GiB a month as an example and shows the real rate when you create the filesystem, so a 2 TB filesystem left behind costs around $400 a month. Ingress and egress are free and stated as such. On-demand instances bill in one-minute increments and are invoiced weekly in arrears, while clusters bill weekly and are paid in advance. Instances are billed for as long as they are running whether or not they are being used, and no stop-and-keep-the-disk state is documented, so the practical choice is to terminate or keep paying the full rate. The smallest realistic monthly bill for a small team is a Quadro RTX 6000 at $503.70 plus a 500 GB filesystem at about $100, so roughly $604 a month with no transfer charges on top.

...

- + Taking a whole eight-GPU H100 node drops the rate to $3.99 per GPU-hour, $2,913 a month per GPU, against $4.29 an hour for a single card.

...

## Pricing

Minimum commitment: $3,132 ($3,132/mo × 1 seat × 1 month (no commitment)). The least you can spend before walking away; excludes numbers, minutes and add-ons.

results.title: Nebius Hikes AI Cloud Prices 21%, Memory Jumps 41% [2026]
results.author: Dr. Heinrich Vogel
highlights:
Nebius just told its customers that AI compute is not getting cheaper. On September 17, 2026, the Amsterdam-based “neocloud” provider notified users it will raise pay-as-you-go prices for Nvidia GPU instances, AMD CPU capacity, and memory starting October 1, 2026. It’s the company’s second price hike in three months, and this time the increases stretch well beyond GPUs into the CPU and memory tiers that most cloud budgets treat as an afterthought.

The numbers are specific. Nvidia H100 instances rise roughly 17%, H200 climbs 20%, B200 goes up about 19%, and the newest B300 chips take the biggest hit at 21%, according to Yahoo Finance’s report on the Nebius announcement. AMD EPYC Genoa CPU rates jump 25%, and memory pricing rises about 41%, the steepest increase across the board. Investors read it as a sign of tight capacity, not weak demand: Nebius shares (Nasdaq: NBIS) jumped as much as 11.1% in pre-market trading the same day.

...

The October 1 price sheet touches nearly every tier of that stack, and in October 2026 Nebius priced H200 GPUs at $5.40/hour and B200 GPUs at $8.50/hour.

...

| Instance type | Price before Oct 1, 2026 | Price from Oct 1, 2026 | Increase |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nvidia H100 (per GPU-hour) | $3.85 | $4.50 | ~17% |
| Nvidia H200 (per GPU-hour) | $4.50 | $5.40 | ~20% |
| Nvidia B200 (per GPU-hour) | $7.15 | $8.50 | ~19% |
| Nvidia B300 (per GPU-hour) | $7.85 | $9.50 | ~21% |
| AMD EPYC Genoa CPU (per vCPU-hour) | Unpublished baseline | $0.015 | ~25% |
| Memory-backed instances | Unpublished baseline | Unpublished | ~41% |

...

Nebius didn’t invent this pattern in September. Around May 2026, the company already raised on-demand capacity prices by an average of 29% and spot capacity by 51%, according to reporting cited by Yahoo Finance’s coverage of the September announcement. Nebius also updated prices for B300, B200, H200 and H100 GPU virtual machines in June 2026. That means Nebius has now raised prices twice in under half a year, with the spot-market increase in the spring actually exceeding the September GPU hikes in percentage terms.

Reuters framed the September move plainly: Nebius is raising prices because demand for computing power keeps rising faster than supply. That’s a different explanation than “costs went up, so we passed them on.” It’s closer to basic capacity rationing, the same mechanism that pushed cloud GPU rental rates up during the original 2023 H100 shortage, except this time it’s spreading into CPU and memory tiers that used to be treated as commodity add-ons.

...

## Nebius vs AWS vs Azure vs Google Cloud vs CoreWeave: Who’s Cheapest Now

Cloud GPU pricing is notoriously hard to compare directly because providers mix spot, on-demand, reserved, and multi-year contract rates on the same public price list. But looking at H100 rental rates across the market as of September 2026 shows just how wide the spread is, and where Nebius now sits after its increase.

| Provider | H100 rate (approx., per GPU-hour) | Billing type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod | $1.99 – $2.99 | On-demand / marketplace |
| Lambda | $3.29 – $3.99 | On-demand |
| Nebius | $4.50 (from Oct 1) | On-demand |
| CoreWeave | $4.25 – $6.16 | On-demand |
| AWS (P5, list price) | ~$6.88 (per-GPU basis) | On-demand |
| Google Cloud | Spot from ~$2.25; on-demand higher | Spot / on-demand |

Data compiled from CloudZero’s 2026 cloud GPU pricing comparison and IntuitionLabs’ Data Center GPU Pricing 2026 index. AWS and Google Cloud figures are derived from multi-GPU instance list prices divided down to a per-GPU basis, so they aren’t perfectly apples-to-apples with single-GPU neocloud rates, but they establish the rough band the market is trading in.

Even after the October 1 increase, Nebius’s $4.50 H100 rate, which a comparison published November 4 still lists as its on-demand price per GPU-hour, lands in the middle of the pack, more expensive than RunPod and Lambda, cheaper than AWS’s list price, and roughly comparable to CoreWeave’s range. That positioning matters: Nebius isn’t pricing itself out of the market, it’s raising prices while staying competitive with the hyperscalers, which is exactly the kind of move a provider makes when it believes customers value reliability and available capacity more than shaving a dollar off the hourly rate.

...

Through 2024 and into 2025, as H100 supply caught up and H200 and early Blackwell systems started shipping, per-GPU rates broadly stabilized and even softened at some specialist providers as competition among neoclouds intensified. That’s part of why the current 2026 landscape shows genuine bargains at providers like RunPod and Lambda sitting well below $4 per H100-hour.

results.title: Tokens per megawatt-hour: the energy economics of frontier AI
results.author: Mehul Kumar
highlights:
At $50 per MWh electricity is 5% of the total; at $120, 11%. A B200 megawatt costs about the same, near $8 million, with 546 GPUs at 1.83 kW of system power each and $45,000 apiece, though each of those chips does several times the work. Facility overhead varies too: Google’s fleet averaged PUE 1.09 in 2025, against the 1.21 assumed here. Renting at assumed on-demand rates of $2.50 to $4 per H100-hour, a range that brackets Lambda’s September 2026 list price of $3.99, would cost $17 to 27 million a year. For context, CoreWeave’s second-quarter 2026 revenue of $2.58 billion comes to about $6.9 million a year per megawatt of the 1.5 GW it had active at the end of June, close to the $7.7 million a year our budget says a megawatt costs to own; it added nearly 500 MW during the quarter, so revenue per megawatt actually in service was higher. Its second-quarter net interest expense of $640 million, annualised, adds roughly $1.7 million per megawatt-year, the financing our budget leaves out. These are company-wide ratios, not H100 rental quotes.

...

The Sonnet list-price scenario implies an 89% margin over the simplified budget; the batch row implies 79%, and renting the chips at Lambda’s $3.99 per GPU-hour list price instead of owning them, 62%. Reported lab margins use different cost boundaries: Anthropic’s inference gross margin was in the mid-sixties per cent in early 2026, by SemiAnalysis’s estimate, and OpenAI’s compute margin on paid products, revenue minus the cost of running its models, was reported at about 70% in October 2025 (The Information, via SaaStr). By May 2026 Anthropic’s gross margin was reported at about 70% on first-quarter results (SaaStr, third-party). Free tiers, flat-rate subscriptions, discounted cached and batch tokens, enterprise deals, cloud rental costs and differences between models all affect the outcome.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Jump 22% in a Month as GPU Shortage Hits Firms and Labs - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: An Hye-ji, Intern Reporter
highlights:
■ Surging GPU costs: Demand for artificial intelligence computing has climbed sharply, prompting domestic cloud providers to raise graphics processing unit rental rates following similar moves by U.S. neocloud companies. Unlike the past, when rental rates for older products fell as new ones arrived, prices for previous-generation GPUs are rising as well, making the ability to secure computing resources a decisive factor in the success of AI businesses and research.

...

- Key summary: Vessl AI, a domestic neocloud company, raised the hourly rate for Nvidia H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39 on the 1st of this month, a 24.7% increase. The price adjustment marks the start of similar moves in Korea after U.S. neocloud firms including CoreWeave and Nebius successively raised GPU rental rates. Vessl AI procures most of its roughly 7,000 GPUs through leasing. According to Ornn, an AI computing trading platform, the hourly cloud rental rate for the H100 rose 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, reaching about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. The impact is spreading to industry and research, with some companies abandoning bids for government-led AI transformation projects because they could not secure GPUs, while universities and research institutes scale back the size of their research.

results.title: Rental Rates for Older AI Chips Jump 25% as Demand Surges - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: Seo Ji-hye, Kim Ji-young
highlights:
Vessl AI raised its hourly rate for Nvidia H100 graphics processing units by 24.7% starting this month, following a string of price increases by U.S. neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius amid a surge in demand for artificial intelligence computing. Supply has tightened not only for the newest chips but also for older models as demand for high-performance GPUs jumps. Other Korean cloud providers also expect to raise GPU rates depending on supply conditions, raising concerns that higher costs of securing GPUs will weigh on service development at Korean AI companies and on government AI transformation, or AX, projects.

Vessl AI on the 1st raised the hourly rate for H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39, according to AI industry sources on the 21st. The neocloud company counts leading Korean AI firms including Upstage and Motif Technologies among its clients and currently operates several thousand GPUs. It has secured about 7,000 GPUs, most of them leased rather than purchased outright. "It is hard to secure the volume we need for H100s — effectively, the price is whatever the seller names," a Vessl AI official said. "As AI demand grows, the number of customers wanting to use GPUs keeps rising, so a price adjustment was unavoidable." The company plans to expand its GPU fleet to about 10,000 units by the end of the year, but intends to keep adjusting rates flexibly to reflect supply conditions and procurement costs.

Other Korean AI cloud companies, including Elice, have also raised prices recently. In the past, rental rates for older AI GPUs fell when new models arrived, but prices for previous-generation chips are now rising as well. Hourly cloud rental rates for the H100 climbed 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, according to Ornn, an AI compute trading platform. That is about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. Analysts say demand is spilling over to relatively older GPUs because supply of the newest chips cannot keep pace with surging computing demand.

results.title: AI Compute Landlords: CoreWeave, Lambda, Neocloud | Humphrey Theodore K. Ng'ambi
highlights:
## Lambda Finances Like a Utility

Lambda tells the capital-structure story most plainly. On 24 August 2026 Bloomberg reported Lambda in talks to raise up to $3 billion at a valuation of $12 billion or more, ahead of a planned 2027 IPO. Three days later Lambda closed a $926 million senior secured Term Loan B led by Morgan Stanley and MUFG, earmarked to buy and install Nvidia GB300 GPUs.

Software companies do not raise money that way. Lambda borrows against GPUs as collateral and layers pre-IPO equity on top — the capital structure of the AI build-out laid bare. Lambda's previous venture valuation was $5.43 billion in November 2025; the pre-IPO round would more than double the number, though Lambda has not confirmed terms.

results.title: Serverless GPU in 2026: What 'Scale to Zero' Really Means, and Where to Run It — Azure, Databricks, Modal, RunPod, Baseten
results.author: Priya Sundaram
highlights:
- 'Serverless GPU' means two different things in 2026, and conflating them is the costly mistake: (1) genuinely serverless = scales to zero, bills per second/minute, costs you nothing when idle; (2) 'rent a GPU by the hour' = a pod/VM that bills even while idle (RunPod Pods, Lambda Labs, CoreWeave). This piece is about category (1).
- The genuinely scale-to-zero options: Azure Container Apps GPU (GA; A100/T4; per-second), Google Cloud Run GPU (GA; L4 only; <5s start), Modal (GA; per-second; best Python DX; ~1s cold start with snapshots), RunPod Serverless (GA; widest GPU menu; <200ms FlashBoot), Baseten (GA; per-minute; production serving, keep a warm floor), and Databricks Serverless GPU compute (still Beta/Preview; A10/H100; DBU-priced).
- On AWS there is no first-party drop-in: Lambda has no GPU and SageMaker Serverless Inference is CPU-only — use SageMaker real-time endpoints or go to Modal/RunPod/Replicate.
- The decision rule: match the platform to your situation, not the sticker price. Python team with bursty custom inference → Modal. Cheapest + widest GPUs + near-instant cold start → RunPod Serverless. Dependable production serving → Baseten. Only need L4 and live on GCP → Cloud Run GPU. Azure enterprise with data-in-boundary rules → Azure Container Apps. Data already in Databricks → Databricks.
- Treat every dollar figure below as approximate — GPU prices move monthly; confirm on the live pricing page before you commit, and never sign a long inference contract at today's rates.

...

| Platform | Scales to zero? | Billing | Example on-demand price (approx — verify) | Cold start (reported) | 2026 status | GPUs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Azure Container Apps GPU | Yes | Per-second | A100 ~$2.34/hr GPU-portion; T4 ~$0.32/hr (full A100 profile ~$8.86/hr) | Tens of sec for big models; cut via artifact streaming | GA | A100, T4 |
| Google Cloud Run GPU | Yes | Per-second | L4 ~$0.67/hr | <5s | GA | L4 only |
| Modal | Yes | Per-second | H100 ~$3.95/hr; A100 80GB ~$2.50/hr; L4 ~$0.80/hr (×1.5–1.75 if region-pinned) | ~5s, ~1s with CPU snapshots | GA | H100/H200/A100/L40S/L4/A10/B200… |
| RunPod Serverless | Yes | Per-second | Flex from ~$0.58/hr; serverless H100 ~$4.55/hr (~2–3× a Pod) | <200ms (FlashBoot) | GA | 30+ incl. H100/H200/B200, RTX 4090, L40S |
| Baseten | Yes (deploy/scale time bills) | Per GPU-minute | A100 80GB ~$4.00/hr; H100 ~$6.50/hr; T4 ~$0.63/hr | Minutes for large models; rec. min 2 replicas | GA | T4, A10G, A100, H100, B200 |
| Databricks Serverless GPU | Yes (on-demand) | DBU-based (no clean per-sec) | Model Serving ~10–628 DBU/hr; DBU ~$0.35–0.95 | Minutes for large models | Beta/Preview (Model Serving GPU is GA) | A10, H100 |
| AWS SageMaker Serverless Inference | Yes | Per-request | — | — | GA but NO GPU (CPU only) | none |
| AWS Lambda | Yes | Per-request | — | — | GA but NO GPU | none |

...

One caveat before the detail: every dollar figure here is approximate. GPU prices move month to month, and the numbers below come from 2026 pricing guides and vendor docs, not a live quote — confirm on each platform's own pricing page before you commit, and never sign a long inference contract at today's rates.

...

### AWS: the gotcha worth stating plainly

If you're on AWS and assumed the serverless primitives would cover GPU, they don't. Lambda has no GPU. SageMaker Serverless Inference is CPU-only. For GPU you use SageMaker real-time or async endpoints (which can scale to zero but aren't pay-per-second serverless), or you leave AWS for Modal/RunPod/Replicate. Don't architect around a SEO blog post claiming otherwise — AWS's own docs are the source of truth here.
